## Module 5 at a glance {#module-5-overview}

**What you will do.** You compare your study samples with a reference set of people from known world regions. You calculate a few numbers for each person that describe their genetic background. You then remove the few samples whose background is very different from the rest.

**What you will learn.**

- Why differences in [ancestry](../docs/glossary.md#ancestry) between cases and controls can create false results.
- How a [principal component](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc) (PC) summarises genetic variation in one number per person.
- How to place study samples on reference axes and draw them in a plot.
- How to flag ancestry outliers with one fixed rule.
- How to choose and justify the number of PCs for the later analysis.

**How long it takes.** About 60 minutes. The slowest step is 5.4, which runs PLINK three times.

## 5.1 Why ancestry matters {#step-5-1}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "This supplied subset has 1,062 samples labelled EUR, AFR, EAS and SAS.", "student_summary": "We count the reference samples in each labelled group. These groups help us compare inherited genetic backgrounds and understand how differences between cases and controls can create false disease associations.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Learn how [population structure](../docs/glossary.md#population-stratification) can mislead an association study. Then look at the reference samples we will use.

### Why

Cases and controls may be recruited from groups with different ancestry. Ancestry means the broad genetic background that a person inherits from their forebears. Then the [allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#allele-frequency) (how common an allele is in a group) can differ between cases and controls, even at sites that have nothing to do with the disease. This is called [confounding](../docs/glossary.md#confounding): a hidden factor is associated with both the group and the genetics.

A principal component (PC) is a single number per person that summarises one main direction of genetic variation across many sites. Principal component analysis (PCA) is the method that finds these directions. PCA only describes patterns. Its axes are not diagnoses, nationality or ethnicity. The reference labels are background information, not a ranking of people. We define an ancestry-matched teaching cohort before we look at any association p-values.

### You need

The saved state from the end of module 4. You also need the supplied GRCh38 [reference subset](../docs/glossary.md#reference-subset), which comes with the course package.

### Command

```{r s5-1}
# 1. Read the reference sample table.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
reference_samples <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".psam"))
# 2. Count the samples in each reference group.
table(reference_samples$SuperPop)
```

### Quick check

Can an allele-frequency difference between cases and controls appear because their ancestry differs, even when the site has no effect on the disease?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Yes. Ancestry can influence both which group a person is in and which alleles that person carries.

</details>

### Files created

<details><summary>Optional: deep dives</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It writes no file in your results folder. It has three deep dives on principal components: what a component is, why genetic data form clusters, and what happens when populations lie on a map. Each deep dive has an example that you can change. The numbers in the examples come from simulated data with a fixed seed.

#### Deep dive: what is a principal component?

**The idea.** Take two measurements for each person, for example height and arm span. The two are correlated, because tall people tend to have a long arm span. The dots form a long, thin cloud. A [principal component](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc) (PC) is the direction along which the dots are most spread out. To see this, draw a line through the middle of the cloud and drop every dot onto the line. The spread of the dropped dots is their variance. Turn the line and the variance changes. The direction with the largest variance is PC1. The line at a right angle to it is PC2. PC2 holds the spread that PC1 does not describe.

{{example:pc-rotation}}

**From two measurements to 100,000 variants.** In genotype data, every variant is one measurement. A person is a point in a space with one axis for each variant. We cannot draw 100,000 axes, but PCA can still find the few directions that carry most of the differences between people. Each person gets one number for each direction. This number is the score. Each variant also gets one weight for each direction. This weight is the loading, and it shows how much the variant contributes to the direction. An [eigenvalue](../docs/glossary.md#eigenvalue) is the variance along one direction. The variance explained is the share of the total variance that one direction holds. The [scree plot](../docs/glossary.md#scree-plot) of step 5.7 shows the eigenvalues in order.

**R code.** The function `demo_rotation_frame()` projects the dots on a line at the angle that you choose. Change `angle` and run the chunk again. The first panel shows your angle. The other four panels show four fixed angles for comparison.

```{r s5-1_dd_rotation, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this angle (in degrees) and run the chunk again.
angle <- 20
data <- demo_rotation_data()
angles <- c(angle, 0, 45, 90, 135)
frames <- lapply(angles, function(a) demo_rotation_frame(data, a))
# Title of each panel: the angle and the share of the total variance on the line.
titles <- sprintf("%d degrees: %.0f%%", angles, 100 * vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$share, numeric(1)))
demo_plot_panels(frames, titles, "People", "Height (cm, centred)", "Arm span (cm, centred)", equal = TRUE)
# The angle of PC1, found by PCA.
demo_rotation_pc1_angle(data)
```

**What to observe.** The share of the variance is largest when the line follows the long direction of the cloud. It is smallest when the line is at a right angle to it. The best angle is the angle of PC1, which the table under the example reports. PCA does the same thing in many dimensions at once.

**Quick check.** Can a turned line ever hold more variance than PC1?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. PC1 is defined as the direction with the largest variance. Every other direction holds the same or less.

</details>

**Reference.** Jolliffe IT, Cadima J. 2016. Principal component analysis: a review and recent developments. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 374:20150202. [doi:10.1098/rsta.2015.0202](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0202).

#### Deep dive: why genetic data form clusters

**The idea.** Two populations that once were one population drift apart. Allele frequencies change by chance in each of them. Fst is a number for how far two populations have drifted. It is 0 when their allele frequencies are the same, and it grows as they differ more. At one variant the difference is tiny, so one variant cannot tell the populations apart. Many variants together can. PCA adds up the small differences of all variants. The populations separate on PC1 only when three things are large enough together: the drift, the number of people and the number of variants. Patterson et al. 2006 call this a phase change. For a fixed data size, a divergence below a threshold is essentially undetectable, and a little above the threshold it is easy to detect. In this example, each population has 100 people.

{{example:fst-snps}}

**R code.** Change `fst` and run the chunk again. The three panels use 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 variants.

```{r s5-1_dd_fst, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. This takes about ten seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this value (0, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01 or 0.05) and run the chunk again.
fst <- 0.005
snps <- c(1000, 10000, 100000)
frames <- demo_fst_frames(fst, snps, seed = 1)
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste(format(snps, big.mark = ","), "variants"), c("Population A", "Population B"))
# Separation of A and B on PC1: 0 means no separation, and a value above 3 is a clear gap.
round(vapply(frames, function(f) f$stats$separation, numeric(1)), 2)
```

**What to observe.** With an Fst of 0, PC1 does not split the two populations, however many variants you use. With a larger Fst, the populations separate, and they separate sooner when you add variants. Near the threshold, more variants turn one blurred cloud into two clusters.

**Quick check.** A study has few variants. PCA shows one cloud for two closely related populations. Does this prove that the populations are the same?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. With this amount of data, a small divergence cannot be seen. More people or more variants could show two clusters.

</details>

**Mixed people.** Some people have ancestors from more than one population. This is admixture. The allele frequencies of a mixed person are a blend of the source populations. PCA places such a person between the sources. In the next example, 40 mixed people have ancestry from populations A and B. A third population, C, is not involved.

{{example:admixture}}

```{r s5-1_dd_admixture, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Each frame takes a few seconds.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change these shares of ancestry from A in the mixed people and run the chunk again.
shares <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)
frames <- lapply(shares, function(s) demo_admixture_frame(s, seed = 1))
demo_plot_panels(frames, paste("Share from A:", shares), c("A", "B", "C", "Mixed A and B"))
```

**What to observe.** The mixed people lie on the line between A and B. They move towards A as the share from A grows. The table under the example compares their mean position with the position expected from their ancestry share.

**Quick check.** A person lies half-way between A and B on the plot. Give one reason, other than admixture, that could place a person there.

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A person from a third population that is genetically between A and B, but that was not sampled, can lie there too. A technical problem with the genotypes can also move a person. A position alone does not show the ancestry.

</details>

**References.** Patterson N, Price AL, Reich D. 2006. Population structure and eigenanalysis. PLoS Genetics 2:e190. [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190).

#### Deep dive: genes and geography

**The idea.** Novembre et al. 2008 ([doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331)) studied people from across Europe. The article reports 3,192 people genotyped at 500,568 variants. The main analysis used 1,387 people and 197,146 variants, because the origin of these people was known with confidence. The origin was the country of all observed grandparents. People whose grandparents came from different countries were left out. We do not reproduce the figures of the article. In words, it reports three things.

- The first two PCs, plotted against each other, look like a map of Europe. People from the same region lie together, and neighbouring regions touch. The authors turned the axes by 16 degrees. They chose this angle because it gave the best match with latitude and longitude.
- The data tell apart Swiss people who speak French, German or Italian.
- The genetic correlation between two people falls as the distance between them grows.

The authors also warn that the direction and the strength of the PC axes depend on how the samples are spread in space. Novembre and Stephens 2008 ([doi:10.1038/ng.139](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.139)) show that smooth gradients across space give regular wave-like patterns in PCA. These patterns do not necessarily show migration events.

Our example is a grid of 36 simulated populations. They are named A1 to F6, and only neighbours exchange migrants. The grid is not a map of any real place. The plot shows the PC1 and PC2 position of each population, and lines join neighbours. PCA does not know where north is, so the raw plot has arbitrary directions. In the turned view we choose the rotation ourselves, knowing the true grid. The method is called Procrustes analysis. It turns, flips and scales the points to match the true places as closely as possible. The table gives the mean error in grid steps.

{{example:stepping-stone}}

**R code.** Change `migration` and run the chunk again. This takes about ten seconds.

```{r s5-1_dd_grid, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes your results folder.
source("R/pca_examples.R")
# Change this migration rate (try 0.8, 0.25, 0.1 or 0.01) and run the chunk again.
migration <- 0.25
uniform <- demo_stepping_stone(migration, "uniform")
corner <- demo_stepping_stone(migration, "corner")
frames <- list(demo_stepping_frame(uniform, turned = FALSE), demo_stepping_frame(uniform, turned = TRUE),
               demo_stepping_frame(corner, turned = TRUE))
demo_plot_panels(frames, c("Raw PCA, uniform sampling", "Turned onto the grid, uniform sampling", "Turned onto the grid, corner sampling"),
                 equal = TRUE, xlab = "East-west (grid steps)", ylab = "North-south (grid steps)")
# Mean error of the population positions, in grid steps: raw, turned, turned with corner sampling.
round(c(uniform$error_raw, uniform$error_turned, corner$error_turned), 2)
```

**What to observe.** With a moderate migration rate, the turned plot recovers the grid. With a very high rate, the populations are so alike that the grid blurs. With a very low rate, each population is nearly an island, and the neighbours no longer lie side by side. With corner sampling, many people come from four populations and few from the others. The sampled corner takes more room, and the rest of the grid is squeezed. The map depends on how we sample.

**Quick check.** Can we say that PC1 points north?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. PCA chooses its axes by variance, not by geography. The sign and the angle depend on the sample. We turned the plot ourselves, using the true grid.

</details>

**References.** Novembre J, et al. 2008. Genes mirror geography within Europe. Nature 456:98-101. [doi:10.1038/nature07331](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07331). Novembre J, Stephens M. 2008. Interpreting principal component analyses of spatial population genetic variation. Nature Genetics 40:646-649. [doi:10.1038/ng.139](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.139).

</details>

## 5.2 Prepare variants for reference PCA {#step-5-2}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "48,615 shared sites are kept for the reference PCA and the projection.", "student_summary": "We find and save the 48,615 sites present in both the cleaned study and the reference. We need the same sites to compare genetic patterns in the two groups.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Find the sites that are present in both the reference subset and the cleaned study. Only common sites on the [autosomes](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) (chromosomes 1 to 22) are used.

### Why

Nearby sites are often inherited together, so they carry the same information. This is called linkage disequilibrium ([LD](../docs/glossary.md#ld)). If PCA uses many such sites, one long correlated stretch can dominate the result. To avoid this, the supplied reference was built with [LD pruning](../docs/glossary.md#ld-pruning), which keeps one site from each correlated group. It kept only common autosomal array sites. It used an [r^2](../docs/glossary.md#r-squared) limit of 0.15 in windows of 200 kb, and it kept at most 50,000 sites.

We keep only the sites that are in both the reference and the study after quality control (QC). We do not add back sites that failed earlier checks. We will prune the sites again later, after we define the final cohort.

### You need

The saved state from step 4.6, and the reference subset supplied at step 0.5.

### Command

```{r s5-2}
# 1. Read the study and reference site tables.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
study_sites <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference_sites <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
# 2. Find the site names that occur in both tables.
common <- sort(intersect(study_sites$ID, reference_sites$ID))
# 3. Save the shared site names and check their number.
guided_list(common, guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
stopifnot(length(common) == 48615L)
cat(length(common), "shared autosomal sites kept\n")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.2", guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"), parent = "4.6")
```

## 5.3 Match build, position and alleles {#step-5-3}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "All 48,615 shared IDs agree on chromosome, GRCh38 position and allele pair.", "student_summary": "We check that each shared site has the same chromosome, DNA position and the two DNA letters that can occur at that site, in both files. This prevents us from comparing different sites that happen to share a name.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Check that the shared variants are really the same variants in both files, before the projection.

### Why

Two variants with the same [rsID](../docs/glossary.md#rsid) (a public name for a variant) are not always the same variant. For each shared variant, check four things: the genome build, the chromosome, the position and the pair of [alleles](../docs/glossary.md#allele). In step 4.5 the array-style names were replaced by IDs made of position and alleles.

If two files list the same two alleles in a different order, the variant is still compatible. If the allele pair differs, or the DNA strand is not resolved, we cannot accept the match without checking. The projection uses the named allele in each weight. It does not use the order of rows in the two files.

### You need

The list of common sites from step 5.2, and the two variant tables (the `.pvar` files) of the study and the reference.

### Command

```{r s5-3}
# 1. Read the shared site names and both site tables.
common <- readLines(guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
ref <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
# 2. Match site names and compare allele pairs in either order.
a <- match(common, study$ID); b <- match(common, ref$ID)
pair <- function(a, b) ifelse(a < b, paste0(a, b), paste0(b, a))
# 3. Check chromosomes, positions and alleles and print the matched count.
stopifnot(all(sub("^chr", "", study$CHROM[a]) == sub("^chr", "", ref$CHROM[b])),
  all(study$POS[a] == ref$POS[b]), all(pair(study$REF[a], study$ALT[a]) == pair(ref$REF[b], ref$ALT[b])))
cat("All", length(common), "shared sites agree on chromosome, position and alleles\n")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

Not applicable: this step needs no PLINK command. The R chunk is the complete command.

R reads or calculates the displayed values without changing the genotype files.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

All 48,615 shared IDs agree on chromosome, GRCh38 position and allele pair. This checks that the two supplied files are compatible. It is not an independent check against a reference genome sequence file (a FASTA file).

<!-- verification_note:start -->The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

### What we do

Calculate the PCs in the reference only. Then place the reference samples and the study samples on the same axes.

### Why

If we ran one PCA on reference and study together, a much larger study group could pull the axes towards itself. So we fix the axes on the reference first. Placing new samples on fixed axes is called [projection](../docs/glossary.md#projection).

Each site has an allele weight (called a loading), which says how much that allele contributes to a PC. The score of a person is the sum of these weights over the alleles the person carries. The reference and the study scores must use the same allele frequencies, the same weights and the same standardisation. Standardisation means rescaling each genotype by the allele frequency, so that common and rare alleles count fairly. The scale and the sign (plus or minus) of a PC are arbitrary. Compare patterns only when both sets of scores use the same scale.

The weight file names the counted allele in a column called [A1](../docs/glossary.md#a1). We switch off mean imputation. This means a missing call is not replaced by the average, so the missing calls stay visible in the score.

### You need

The checked shared sites from step 5.3, and the full saved state from step 4.6.

### Command

```{r s5-4}
# 1. Set the reference input, shared site list and output names.
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
common <- guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt")
fit <- guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "reference")
# 2. Calculate ten reference components and save their allele contributions.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, "--freq", "--pca", "10", "allele-wts", "--out", fit))
# 3. Find the columns containing site names, alleles and component contributions.
weights <- guided_table(paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"))
id_column <- match("ID", names(weights)); allele_column <- match("A1", names(weights))
first_pc <- match("PC1", names(weights))
# 4. Prepare the same reference frequencies and scoring rules for both groups.
score <- c("--read-freq", paste0(fit, ".afreq"), "--score", paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"),
  id_column, allele_column, "header-read", "no-mean-imputation", "variance-standardize",
  "--score-col-nums", paste0(first_pc, "-", first_pc + 9L))
# 5. Place the reference samples on the fixed reference axes.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores")))
# 6. Place the study samples on the same reference axes.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores")))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.4", c(paste0(fit, c(".afreq", ".eigenvec", ".eigenval", ".eigenvec.allele")), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore")), parent = "5.2")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --freq --pca 10 allele-wts --out results/guided/s5-4_reference --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_ref_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_study_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--extract` keeps only the checked shared sites. `--freq` writes the allele frequencies of the reference. `--pca 10 allele-wts` computes ten axes and saves the allele weights. `--read-freq` gives the same frequencies to both projections. `--score` names the weight file and the columns that hold the variant ID and the A1 allele (columns 2 and 5 here, counted from one). `header-read` tells PLINK to use the header line of the weight file. `no-mean-imputation` stops PLINK replacing missing calls with the average. `variance-standardize` scales the genotypes with the allele frequencies. `--score-col-nums 6-15` selects PC1 to PC10. The R command finds these column numbers from the real header line. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Reference eigenvectors and eigenvalues, allele weights, and two `.sscore` files (score tables) with the columns PC1_AVG to PC10_AVG. The study projection contains 1,844 samples.

`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

</details>

</details>

### Quick check

Why must the study projection use the reference frequencies, and not recalculate the standardisation from the study alone?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Otherwise the two sets of scores would not share the same coordinate system.

</details>

### Files created

`s5-4_reference.*`, `s5-4_ref_scores.sscore`, `s5-4_study_scores.sscore` and logs.

<details><summary>Under the hood & literature</summary>

**What the tool computes.** `--pca 10 allele-wts` finds the top ten principal components of the reference genotypes after each variant is shifted to mean 0 and scaled to variance 1 with its allele frequency. The `.eigenvec.allele` file has one line per allele. After the variant ID and `A1`, each `PC` column is the weight of that allele on that component. `--score` then gives each person the average of weight times standardised genotype over the shared alleles. The `_AVG` columns are averages, so their scale differs from the `.eigenvec` file. Use the projected scores for both groups.

**Why these values.** Ten components is PLINK's default and a course convention. Step 5.7 fixes how many enter the model. `--read-freq` gives both groups the same frequencies. `no-mean-imputation` leaves missing calls out of the average.

**Pitfalls.** Projected study samples shrink towards the origin, and the bias grows from PC5 onwards, so read distances on later PCs with care. An allele that does not match by name contributes nothing, so the score silently uses fewer sites. At an A/T or C/G site, a strand flip keeps the name but reverses the meaning and flips the sign of its contribution. This is why the shared sites are checked at step 5.3. A person from an ancestry absent from the reference tends to land near the closest reference group. The spelling `variance-standardize` is American; the course text says standardise.

**References**

1. Patterson N et al. (2006) Population structure and eigenanalysis. PLoS Genet 2:e190. PMID 17194218.
2. Price AL et al. (2006) Principal components analysis corrects for stratification in genome-wide association studies. Nat Genet 38:904-909. PMID 16862161.
3. Privé F et al. (2020) Efficient toolkit implementing best practices for principal component analysis of population genetic data. Bioinformatics 36:4449-4457. PMID 32415959.
4. The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium (2015) A global reference for human genetic variation. Nature 526:68-74. PMID 26432245.

</details>

## 5.5 Plot the reference and projected study {#step-5-5}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "A labelled plot of the reference with the projected study.", "student_summary": "We plot the first three principal components, each a number summarising one pattern of genetic variation, in three pairs. We show reference groups with labels and symbols and add the study samples to see how their genetic backgrounds compare.", "student_plink_options": []} -->
### What we do

Draw three plots of the first three reference axes: PC1 against PC2, PC1 against PC3 and PC2 against PC3. Each reference group has its own label and symbol, and the study samples are added on top. All three plots use the same symbols, colours and key.

### Why

A plot of two PCs helps us see large differences between samples. Later PCs can show patterns that PC1 and PC2 hide. This is why we also plot PC3 against each of the first two. A difference can also come from the genotyping platform, from missing data or from allele errors. The study points are projected scores. They are not a separate PCA. The groups use symbols as well as colour, so the plot stays readable without colour.

### You need

The score files from step 5.4, and the reference sample table.

### Command

```{r s5-5}
# 1. Read both score tables and the reference group labels.
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
# 2. Match the reference labels to samples and choose group symbols and colours.
group <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)]
levels <- sort(unique(group)); code <- match(group, levels)
colours <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00")
# 3. Define one plotting function, so that all pictures use the same symbols, colours and key.
plot_components <- function(x, y, file) {
  png(file, width = 1400, height = 850, res = 140)
  par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 4, 9))
  plot(as.numeric(ref[[paste0("PC", x, "_AVG")]]), as.numeric(ref[[paste0("PC", y, "_AVG")]]), col = colours[code], pch = code,
    xlab = paste0("Reference PC", x, " score"), ylab = paste0("Reference PC", y, " score"),
    main = paste0("GRCh38 reference and projected simulated study: PC", x, " and PC", y))
  # Add the study samples and a key for the groups. The key sits outside the plot, on the right, so it hides no points.
  points(as.numeric(study[[paste0("PC", x, "_AVG")]]), as.numeric(study[[paste0("PC", y, "_AVG")]]), pch = 20, cex = 0.4, col = "#333333")
  legend("topright", inset = c(-0.21, 0), xpd = TRUE, legend = c(levels, "Study projection"), col = c(colours[seq_along(levels)], "#333333"), pch = c(seq_along(levels), 20), cex = 0.8)
  invisible(dev.off())
}
# 4. Save the picture for PC1 and PC2, then the two extra pictures for PC1 and PC3 and for PC2 and PC3.
files <- c(guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection_pc1_pc3.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection_pc2_pc3.png"))
plot_components(1, 2, files[1]); plot_components(1, 3, files[2]); plot_components(2, 3, files[3])
# 5. Print the location of each picture.
for (file in files) cat("The plot was saved to ", file, "\n", sep = "")
```

### Optional: a 3D plot with ellipses

<details><summary>Show the optional 3D plot</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. The code is not run by default. It draws the three first components in one rotating 3D picture. A 95% ellipse is drawn around each reference group. An ellipse shows where about 95% of the points of a group are expected to lie. The code needs the package `rgl`, which step 0.5 does not install. To install it once, type `install.packages("rgl")` in the R console. On macOS, `rgl` may also need the free program XQuartz. If the package does not install, or no window opens, skip this box. The code does nothing when `rgl` is missing.

```{r s5-5_optional_3d, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Needs the rgl package: install.packages("rgl")
if (requireNamespace("rgl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # 1. Collect the scores of the first three components for the reference samples.
  scores <- cbind(as.numeric(ref$PC1_AVG), as.numeric(ref$PC2_AVG), as.numeric(ref$PC3_AVG))
  # 2. Draw the reference samples in 3D, with the colours used in the 2D plots.
  rgl::plot3d(scores, col = colours[code], size = 4, xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", zlab = "PC3")
  # 3. Add one 95% ellipse for each reference group.
  for (i in seq_along(levels)) {
    group_scores <- scores[code == i, , drop = FALSE]
    rgl::plot3d(rgl::ellipse3d(cov(group_scores), centre = colMeans(group_scores), level = 0.95),
      col = colours[i], alpha = 0.15, add = TRUE)
  }
} else {
  message("The rgl package is not installed. Skip this optional plot.")
}
```

</details>

## 5.6 Define an ancestry-matched cohort {#step-5-6}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain.", "student_summary": "We compare each study sample with a European reference group on the first four principal components, numbers that summarise patterns of genetic variation. We remove a sample if any of them lies more than six standard deviations (a measure of spread) from the reference mean; this rule defines the group for our teaching analysis.", "student_plink_options": [{"label": "remove samples outside the reference rule", "options": [{"name": "--pfile", "explanation": "Reads the cleaned study genotype files s4-6_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam from the results folder."}, {"name": "--remove", "explanation": "Removes the samples listed in s5-6_remove.txt because at least one of their first four component scores is more than six standard deviations from the European reference mean."}, {"name": "--make-pgen", "explanation": "Saves the retained 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files."}, {"name": "--out", "explanation": "Starts the retained study output file names with s5-6_state."}]}]} -->
### What we do

Apply a rule, fixed in advance, to the first four projected PCs. The rule flags samples that are more than six standard deviations from the European reference.

### Why

In this teaching design, the main analysis uses a cohort that broadly matches the European reference. The rule has three parts. First, take the European reference samples. For each of PC1 to PC4, calculate their mean and their [standard deviation](../docs/glossary.md#standard-deviation) (a measure of how spread out the values are). Second, convert each study score into a distance from that mean, counted in standard deviations. Third, flag a sample as an [outlier](../docs/glossary.md#outlier) if its largest distance, ignoring the sign, is above six.

This is a rule for this study only. It is not a general way to classify ancestry. Apply it before you look at any association results, and report who was excluded.

### You need

The reference and study scores from step 5.4, and the reference labels used in step 5.5.

### Command

```{r s5-6}
# 1. Read the reference and study scores and reference group labels.
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
# 2. Select the European reference samples and the first four component scores.
eur <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)] == "EUR"
columns <- paste0("PC", 1:4, "_AVG")
r <- sapply(ref[eur, columns, drop = FALSE], as.numeric)
s <- sapply(study[columns], as.numeric)
# 3. Measure each study score's distance from the reference mean using its spread.
centre <- colMeans(r)
spread <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(r, 2, centre, "-")^2))
z <- sweep(sweep(s, 2, centre, "-"), 2, spread, "/")
# 4. List samples more than six standard deviations away on any selected component.
bad <- study$IID[apply(abs(z), 1, max) > 6]
remove <- guided_list(bad, guided_path(cfg, "5.6", "remove.txt"), TRUE)
# 5. Remove the listed samples and save the retained study group.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--remove", remove, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.6")))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "5.6", "4.6")
guided_register(cfg, "5.6", "5.4", 1811, 238513, operations = ops)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --remove results/guided/s5-6_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s5-6_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

R applies the rule and writes the list of flagged sample IDs (IIDs). `--remove` takes out the samples on that list from the full study data. `--make-pgen` saves the retained cohort. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain. Some of the simulated outliers were already removed in earlier QC steps. So 33 is not the total number of outliers in the original data.

</details>

### Quick check

Why does the rule use four PCs and not only the two shown in the plot?

</details>

### Files created

<details><summary>Try other thresholds (optional)</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It does not change your results.

The course removes a study sample when it lies more than six standard deviations (SD) from the mean of the European reference on any of the first four PCs. The first table changes the number of SD. The second table is an alternative method (see the box "Another approach"): the robust Mahalanobis distance with a cutoff at a quantile of the chi-squared distribution. It has no course value. Each trial starts from the 1,844 study samples of step 4.6.

```{r s5-6_thresholds, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.6. The package MASS comes with R.
# 1. Read the scores of step 5.4 and apply the methods to the same samples.
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
result <- ancestry_outliers(ref, study, metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)])
# 2. Change the number of SD of the course rule.
sd_trial <- outlier_sd_counts(result, c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8))
sd_trial$course_value <- sd_trial$threshold == 6
# 3. Change the chi-squared quantile of the robust Mahalanobis distance.
mcd_trial <- outlier_mcd_counts(result, c(0.99, 0.999, 0.9999))
mcd_trial$course_value <- FALSE
sd_trial
mcd_trial
# 4. Plot the removed samples.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot_threshold_trials(sd_trial, "Samples removed", log_x = FALSE); plot_threshold_trials(mcd_trial, "Samples removed", log_x = FALSE)
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```

Plain PLINK 2 command: not applicable. R reads the score tables and calculates the distances.

The expected result of the trials:

Study samples removed by the course rule when the number of SD changes:

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 34 | 1,810 |
| 5 | 33 | 1,811 |
| **6 (course value)** | 33 | 1,811 |
| 7 | 33 | 1,811 |
| 8 | 33 | 1,811 |

Study samples removed by the robust Mahalanobis distance (alternative method):

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.99 | 86 | 1,758 |
| 0.999 | 39 | 1,805 |
| 0.9999 | 34 | 1,810 |

How to read it. The number of SD hardly matters. From 5 to 8 SD the rule removes the same 33 samples, and 4 SD adds one. The 33 samples are far from the European cluster, so any sensible limit finds them. The distance method depends much more on its cutoff. At the 99% point it removes 86 samples, at 99.9% it removes 39 and at 99.99% it removes 34. The extra samples are at the edge of the European cluster, so a loose cutoff removes people of European ancestry. At 99.99% the method nearly agrees with the course rule.

Expected plot. For `SD limit`, the horizontal axis shows the setting and the vertical axis shows the number of samples removed. A red diamond marks the course value (6), where 33 samples are removed. For `MCD chi-squared quantile`, the horizontal axis shows the setting and the vertical axis shows the number of samples removed. This is an alternative method, so the plot has no course value. The line joins the points in the order of the settings. The same plot with ggplot2 looks the same and has a light grid.

</details>

<details><summary>Another approach (optional)</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It writes only to files that start with `s5-6_alt_`, so the files and checkpoints of the main path do not change.

The course rule is simple. A sample is an outlier when it lies more than six standard deviations from the mean of the European reference on any of the first four PCs. Two other methods are common. This box runs all three on the same samples and compares them.

**Robust Mahalanobis distance (MCD).** The Mahalanobis distance measures how far a sample is from the centre of a group, and it takes the shape of the group into account. A plain centre can be pulled away by outliers. The minimum covariance determinant (MCD) method finds the centre and the shape from the most compact part of the group, so the outliers cannot move them. A sample is an outlier when its squared distance is above the 99.9% point of a chi-squared distribution with four degrees of freedom (one degree for each PC), which is 18.47. We use the function `cov.rob` of the package MASS, which is installed with R. When to prefer it: when the reference group is small or its shape is not round, because the distance follows the shape.

**Nearest 1000 Genomes group.** The step 5.4 scores place the study samples in the same space as the reference. This method measures the Mahalanobis distance of each study sample to the centre of each of the four reference groups (AFR, EAS, EUR and SAS) and assigns the sample to the nearest one. A sample is an outlier when its nearest group is not EUR. When to prefer it: when you want to know where each outlier comes from, for example to keep a second ancestry group for a separate analysis.

```{r s5-6_alternatives, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.6. The package MASS comes with R.
# 1. Read the scores of step 5.4 and the group of each reference sample.
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
group <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)]
# 2. Apply the three methods to the same samples and compare them.
result <- ancestry_outliers(ref, study, group)
outlier_method_table(result)
# 3. Save a plot with a different symbol for the samples that each method removes.
plot_outlier_methods(result, guided_path(cfg, "5.6", "alt_methods.png"))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command: not applicable. R reads the score tables and calculates the distances. It does not change the genotype files.

Expected result. The table has one row for each method.

| Method | Samples removed | In common with the 6 SD rule | Only this method | Missed by this method |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 SD rule (course) | 33 | 33 | 0 | 0 |
| Robust Mahalanobis (MCD) | 39 | 33 | 6 | 0 |
| Nearest 1000 Genomes group | 33 | 33 | 0 | 0 |

The plot shows an orange triangle, a blue square and a black cross around the samples that each method removes. The 33 samples that all three methods remove form three small groups far from the European cluster. The six extra samples of the MCD method are blue squares at the edge of the European cluster.

How to read it. The six extra MCD samples are not ancestry outliers. Their largest distance on a single PC is between 2.3 and 4.3 standard deviations, and their squared Mahalanobis distance is between 18.8 and 24.6, just above the cutoff of 18.47. The real outliers have a squared distance of at least 2,866. With a cutoff at the 99.9% point, we expect about 0.1% of a perfectly normal group to be flagged. Here that is about 1.8 of the 1,811 European-like samples, and the method flags 6. This is why the course keeps the six-SD rule: the European cluster of this dataset is large and homogeneous, and the distance cutoff is too tight for it. The nearest-group method gives the same 33 samples as the course rule, so here it adds a label (where each outlier comes from) and no new samples.

References. Six standard deviations on the first PCs: Price et al. 2006, [doi:10.1038/ng1847](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng1847). The MCD estimator: Rousseeuw and Van Driessen 1999, [doi:10.1080/00401706.1999.10485670](https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1999.10485670). Outlier detection in PCA of genetic data: Privé et al. 2020, [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520). Assigning people to ancestry groups with a reference: Privé et al. 2022, [doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.11.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.11.008).

</details>

## 5.7 Cohort PCs and how many to include {#step-5-7}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "Ten cohort PCs, a scree plot and a complete saved state for step 5.7 with 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants.", "student_summary": "We select common sites with weaker correlations and calculate ten principal components, each a number summarising one pattern of genetic variation within the retained study group. ### What we do

Calculate new PCs in the retained study cohort, look at the eigenvalues and save the full state.

### Why

The reference axes describe broad differences between world regions. PCs calculated inside the cohort can capture finer differences that matter for association. We prune the sites again, because the cohort has changed. We keep only common sites, which means a [minor allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#maf) (MAF, the frequency of the rarer allele) of at least 0.05.

An [eigenvalue](../docs/glossary.md#eigenvalue) measures how much variation one PC explains. A [scree plot](../docs/glossary.md#scree-plot) shows the eigenvalues in order, from the largest to the smallest.

The long-range LD regions are the same as in step 3.4. The list follows the collection of Grinde et al. 2024 ([doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242)). The course fixes the number of PCs at ten for the main model. We do not choose the number to get attractive p-values. Too few PCs can leave confounding in the results. Too many PCs can reduce the precision of the estimates. In module 7 we compare other numbers of PCs as a sensitivity check. We do not use that check to search for the most significant result.

### You need

The retained cohort from step 5.6, and the list of GRCh38 long-range LD regions to exclude.

### Command

```{r s5-7}
# 1. Prepare the regions to exclude and the site selection output name.
regions <- guided_high_ld(cfg)
prune <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "prune")
# 2. Select common sites on chromosomes 1 to 22 with weaker correlations with each other.
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--chr", "1-22", "--maf", "0.05", "--exclude", "bed0", regions,
  "--indep-pairwise", "200kb", "0.2", "--out", prune))
# 3. Calculate ten components within the retained study group using the selected sites.
report <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--extract", paste0(prune, ".prune.in"), "--pca", "10", "--out", report))
# 4. Read how much variation each component explains and plot these values.
eigenvalues <- scan(paste0(report, ".eigenval"), quiet = TRUE)
png(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), width = 1000, height = 700, res = 130)
plot(seq_along(eigenvalues), eigenvalues, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "PC number", ylab = "Eigenvalue", main = "Retained cohort: first ten PCs")
# 5. Finish saving the picture and print its location.
invisible(dev.off())
cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), "\n", sep = "")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_snapshot(cfg, "5.7", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), 1811, 238513, parent = "5.6")
file.copy(paste0(report, c(".eigenvec", ".eigenval")), file.path(cfg$out, "checkpoints", "5.7"), overwrite = TRUE)
check_step("5.7", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --chr 1-22 --maf 0.05 --exclude bed0 results/guided/s3-4_high_ld.bed0 --indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2 --out results/guided/s5-7_prune --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-7_prune.prune.in --pca 10 --out results/guided/s5-7_pca --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--maf 0.05` keeps only common sites for the pruning. `--chr 1-22` keeps only autosomal sites. `--exclude bed0` skips the long-range LD regions listed in a BED file. A BED file counts the start of a region from 0 and does not include its end. `--indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2` writes the list of sites left after pruning, using windows of 200 kb and an r^2 limit of 0.2. `--extract` uses that list only for the PCA. `--pca 10` computes the ten cohort eigenvectors. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Ten cohort PCs, a scree plot and a complete saved state for step 5.7 with 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants. The first cohort eigenvalue is about 14. The signs of the eigenvectors can differ on your computer. This does not change how the PCs adjust the association. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

<!-- verification_note:start -->The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.<!-- verification_note:end -->

if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)

### Quick check

Should we choose the number of PCs by trying many models and keeping the one with the most genome-wide significant hits?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. Fix the main model before you see any association result. Report the sensitivity analyses openly.

</details>

### Files created

Pruning lists, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, the scree plot (PNG), the working state and the full 5.7 checkpoint.

<details><summary>Try other thresholds (optional)</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It does not change your results.

The course keeps ten PCs as covariates. This box repeats the association scan with 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 PCs and shows how many hits and which lambda each choice gives. It runs its own 20-component PCA and writes only to files that start with `s5-7_alt_`. The box takes about three minutes, because it runs PLINK eight times. See also the box "Another approach", which shows the scree plot and the PCs that are associated with the outcome.

```{r s5-7_thresholds, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.7. This takes about three minutes.
trials <- guided_pc_trials(cfg)
trials$trials
# Plot lambda and the number of hits against the number of PCs.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$lambda, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Lambda", main = "Lambda"); abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$hits, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Hits below 5e-8", main = "Hits")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command: the function runs `--pca 20` on the pruned list of step 5.7, and then `--glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback` once for each number of PCs, with the same options as step 6.3.

The expected result of the trials:

| Number of PCs | Hits below 5e-8 | Lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 17 | 1.5273 |
| 1 | 8 | 1.0101 |
| 2 | 8 | 1.0136 |
| 3 | 8 | 1.0137 |
| 5 | 8 | 1.0150 |
| **10 (course value)** | 8 | 1.0157 |
| 15 | 8 | 1.0185 |
| 20 | 8 | 1.0183 |

How to read it. Without PCs, there are 17 hits and lambda is 1.527, so the correction is needed. One PC already brings lambda to 1.010. Ten PCs give 1.016, and 15 and 20 PCs give 1.018. The number of hits stays at eight from one PC on. In this dataset only PC1 carries ancestry, so more PCs add only a little noise.

Expected plot. The horizontal axis shows the number of PCs. The left plot shows lambda, which falls from 1.53 to about 1.01 with one PC and then rises slowly to 1.02. The right plot shows the number of hits, which falls from 17 to 8 with one PC and then stays at 8. The course value is ten PCs, with 8 hits and lambda 1.016.

</details>

<details><summary>Another approach (optional)</summary>

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It runs its own PCA with 20 components and its own association scans, and it writes only to files that start with `s5-7_alt_`. The files and checkpoints of the main path do not change. The box takes about three minutes, because it runs PLINK eight times.

The course keeps ten PCs. This box shows how to decide how many PCs a study needs. Three ideas help.

- **The scree plot.** The eigenvalue of a PC shows how much variation it carries. PCs that carry real structure stand above a flat tail. The bend between the two parts, the elbow, suggests how many to keep.
- **PCs associated with the outcome.** A PC that differs between cases and controls can confound the test. We test each PC against the disease with a logistic regression. A PC that is not associated with the outcome adds little to the correction.
- **The inflation factor.** We repeat the association scan with 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 PCs, and we read lambda and the number of hits. Lambda should be close to 1.

A formal test also exists. The Tracy-Widom test asks whether an eigenvalue is larger than expected from random noise (Patterson et al. 2006, [doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.0020190)). We do not run it here.

One more point concerns the regions that we exclude before the PCA. Leaving out the long-range LD regions is common advice, and the course follows it. It does not remove every problem, though. Grinde et al. 2024 ([doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011242)) studied samples of African American people, who have mixed ancestry. They found that later PCs can describe small parts of the genome instead of ancestry. Adjusting for such a PC can create a false link between a variant and the disease. This problem is called collider bias. A collider is a variable that two other things both influence. When a model adjusts for it, those two things can look related when they are not. Excluding the known long-range LD regions did not solve it in their data, and LD pruning worked better. In our cohort the risk is smaller. Everyone belongs to one European cluster, and only PC1 carries ancestry (see the table below). Still, a good habit is to check what each PC describes, for example by plotting its loadings along the genome, before you add it to a model.

```{r s5-7_pc_number, eval=FALSE}
# Optional. Nothing here changes the files of step 5.7. This takes about three minutes.
# 1. Run a 20-component PCA and the association scans for 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 20 PCs.
trials <- guided_pc_trials(cfg)
# 2. Show hits and lambda for each number of PCs.
trials$trials
# 3. Show the first eigenvalues and the p-values of the first PCs against the outcome.
round(trials$eigenvalues[1:5], 3)
signif(trials$outcome_p[1:5], 3)
# 4. Plot the eigenvalues (scree plot) and lambda against the number of PCs.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(1:20, trials$eigenvalues, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "PC number", ylab = "Eigenvalue", main = "Scree plot")
plot(trials$trials$k, trials$trials$lambda, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "Number of PCs", ylab = "Lambda", main = "Lambda")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command: the function runs `--pca 20` on the pruned list of step 5.7, and then `--glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback` once for each number of PCs, with the same options as step 6.3. The covariates are Age and the first k PCs (`--covar-name Age,PC1-PC10` for ten).

Expected result.

| Number of PCs | Hits below 5e-8 | Lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 17 | 1.5273 |
| 1 | 8 | 1.0101 |
| 2 | 8 | 1.0136 |
| 3 | 8 | 1.0137 |
| 5 | 8 | 1.0150 |
| **10 (course value)** | 8 | 1.0157 |
| 15 | 8 | 1.0185 |
| 20 | 8 | 1.0183 |

The scree plot has one high point and a flat tail. The first eigenvalue is 13.996, and the second is 1.428. The p-values against the outcome are 2.3e-17 for PC1, 0.054 for PC2 and 0.59 for PC3.

How to read it. Only PC1 stands out. Its eigenvalue is ten times larger than the rest, and it is the only PC with a clear association with the outcome. Without any PC, there are 17 hits and lambda is 1.53, so the correction is needed. One PC already brings lambda to 1.010. Ten PCs give 1.016 and 20 give 1.018, so extra PCs do not help and add a little noise. The number of hits stays at eight. The course keeps ten PCs because it is a common default and it is safe, and this dataset shows that fewer would also work. For a real study, choose the number from the scree plot and the lambda, and report it.

</details>


## Module 5 recap {#module-5-recap}

- You compared the study with a GRCh38 reference subset of 1,062 samples.
- You kept 48,615 shared sites, and all of them matched on chromosome, position and alleles.
- You placed 1,844 study samples on the reference axes and drew the plot.
- You applied the six-standard-deviation rule and excluded 33 outlier records.
- 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain, with ten cohort PCs ready for the association model.

**Next:** module 6, where you run the association test and use these PCs as covariates.
